docs.title: ktor-guard
docs.text:
Ktor 3.x adapter for the guard-core-jvm engine for the JVM. ktor-guard is a true port of the guard adapter pattern (fastapi-guard's SecurityMiddleware, JVM-idiomized for Ktor 3.x): it wraps Ktor ApplicationCall into the guard-core-jvm facade protocols and drives the engine's security pipeline per request through suspend-native Ktor server plugin hooks. It contains no security logic of its own; every decision is the engine's.

  • Status: 1.0.0, released (the first synchronized release)
  • Engine: com.guard-core:guard-core:4.3.3 (built from source through a composite build, see Installation)
  • Stack: Ktor 3.x (built and tested against 3.6.0), Kotlin 2.4.21, JDK 17, suspend-native (the facade's suspend APIs are called directly)
  • Parity: the engine's every-feature matrix and the spec section table carry the family-level status

docs.title: Adapter parity: fastapi-guard 8.1.0 (PureASGISecurityMiddleware)
docs.text: Assessment of the W10 parity wave (2026-10-13): what fastapi-guard 8.1.0 changed, how this adapter's native idiom maps onto it, and which of the pure-streaming properties hold here. Conclusion up front: all three pure-streaming properties already hold natively; zero code changes.

docs.title: What upstream shipped
docs.text:
fastapi-guard 8.1.0 (2026-10-10, #156) added PureASGISecurityMiddleware: the full screening pipeline running on raw ASGI without BaseHTTPMiddleware. It exists to win three properties the classic middleware loses to Starlette's anyio task group:

  1. No downstream wrapping that could cancel in-flight work (a client disconnect can never cancel an in-flight database call).
  2. Unbuffered response streaming (security and CORS headers injected directly on http.response.start, body bytes never held).
  3. A caching receive that replays the request body to the application after the guard reads it.

Scope note from the upstream release: decorator-driven response rules (return patterns) and custom_response_modifier need a materialized Response object; they stay on the classic middleware and both classes ship side by side.

docs.title: The idiom mapping
docs.text: This adapter's native idiom is the Ktor server plugin: the request side is a custom Hook intercepting the Plugins phase (GuardRequestHook), the response side is the ResponseBodyReadyForSend hook, and a block short-circuits with finish() so the route handler never starts. Ktor never had a BaseHTTPMiddleware analog: the plugin's hooks run on the framework's own call pipeline, which is the shape PureASGI was built to reach. The upstream release validates an idiom this adapter has used since W6.

docs.title: 1. No downstream cancelling wrap: HOLDS
docs.text: The plugin adds no wrapping of its own: GuardRequestHook runs its checks inside the call pipeline intercept, then returns and lets the handler execute in the framework's own coroutine (the dispatch comment in GuardCorePlugin.kt: "the call_next leg ... Ktor's suspend dispatch performs after this hook returns"). There is no middleware-owned coroutine scope around the downstream code, so there is no middleware-induced cancellation surface; the only cancellation source is the engine's own native semantics. On a block, the hook finishes the pipeline before the handler starts, mirroring the reference dispatch ordering.

docs.title: 2. Unbuffered response streaming: HOLDS
docs.text: The response hook materializes body bytes only for OutgoingContent.ByteArrayContent (materializeBody); streamed bodies (WriteChannelContent and friends) are never read. Streamed responses get additions only - header appends (engine-managed headers skipped) and a status change through the response status channel (reflectStreamed, documented in-code since W6: "Streamed bodies: header additions and a status change only (no replayable body)"). Buffered bodies (respondText/respondBytes) rebuild the content with the full processed header set, so behavioral return rules and the response modifier carry exactly on them - the same scoping decision as the upstream scope note (the features that need a materialized response get one; the features that do not, never hold the bytes).

docs.title: 3. A caching receive that replays the body: HOLDS
docs.text: KtorGuardRequest drains the request body exactly once (bounded, under the facade's read timeout), caches the bytes, and installs the drained body back as the call's receive channel, so the route handler observes the same full body the scan saw while repeat reads never re-consume the stream (the documented bounded-read replay contract, the Ktor idiom for the reference's replaying receive).

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text: Zero code changes in the 8.1.0 parity wave. The Ktor hook idiom already satisfies the pure-streaming properties PureASGISecurityMiddleware was built to win: no downstream wrap, streamed bodies untouched (additions only), and a replaying cached receive.

docs.title: API
docs.text: The adapter's public surface (package com.guardcore.ktor). Consumers import from the adapter package, never from the engine coordinates directly.

docs.title: GuardCore (the server plugin)
docs.text:
install(GuardCore) at the Plugins phase gives the required short-circuit: a pipeline block responds with the engine's byte-exact error shape and the route handler never executes (proven by a dedicated test). Configuration:

install(GuardCore) {
    config = SecurityConfigBuilder().apply { /* ... */ }.build()
    decorator = GuardRouteDecorator(config)   // optional per-route config
}

Per-request behavior (mirroring the reference adapter exactly): lazy single-flight init with the 503 + Retry-After: 5 Redis path; the call wraps into the facade GuardRequest (bounded body reads with replay to the handler); CORS preflight; path exclusions (fail-secure 403 when no client address resolves under fail_secure); client-IP resolution through the engine (trusted_proxies, X-Forwarded-For chain, X-Forwarded-Proto); route configuration resolves per request from the stamped route id; the 17-check fixed-order pipeline; behavioral usage rules for decorated routes; and the response exit path (metrics, security headers, CORS headers, behavioral return rules, custom response modifier).

Eager init: install(GuardCore) initializes on ServerReady with a single-flight mutex.

docs.title: GuardRouteDecorator
docs.text:
GuardRouteDecorator carries the facade SecurityDecorator factories 1:1 (same parameter surface, route key bound by the extension). Grouped blocks mirror the Python mixins:

get("/limited") { call.respondText("limited") }
    .guardRateLimit(guard, requests = 5, window = 60)

get("/admin") { call.respondText("admin") }
    .guard(guard) {
        requireIp(whitelist = listOf("10.0.0.1"))
    }

25/25 decorator factories are available, mirroring the facade class exactly.

docs.title: Re-exports
docs.text: GuardCoreExports.kt re-exports the engine's user-facing types (the fastapi-guard guard/__init__.py convention): SecurityConfig, SecurityConfigBuilder, SecurityDecorator, RouteConfig, the handler managers, and the protocol types.

docs.title: Response handling
docs.text: The response side hooks ResponseBodyReadyForSend: the buffered mode is the exact Starlette replacement semantics (byte-exact header/body shaping); streaming responses are additions only (headers + behavioral scan where the bounded reader yields a prefix).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
examples/demo-ktor is a runnable Ktor server with guarded and open routes, live Redis-backed per-route rate limiting, and the handler-ran-never proof for blocked requests.

git clone https://github.com/Guard-Core/ktor-guard.git
cd ktor-guard
git clone https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core-jvm.git guard-core-jvm
git -C guard-core-jvm checkout 7711606
docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine
./gradlew :examples:demo-ktor:run

Minimal integration in your own app:

import com.guardcore.ktor.GuardCore
import com.guardcore.ktor.GuardRouteDecorator
import com.guardcore.ktor.SecurityConfigBuilder
import com.guardcore.ktor.guard
import com.guardcore.ktor.guardRateLimit
import io.ktor.server.application.install
import io.ktor.server.engine.embeddedServer
import io.ktor.server.cio.CIO
import io.ktor.server.response.respondText
import io.ktor.server.routing.get
import io.ktor.server.routing.routing

fun main() {
    val config = SecurityConfigBuilder().apply {
        blockedUserAgents = listOf("badbot")
        enableRateLimiting = true
    }.build()

    val guard = GuardRouteDecorator(config)

    embeddedServer(CIO, port = 8080) {
        install(GuardCore) {
            this.config = config
            this.decorator = guard
        }
        routing {
            get("/public") { call.respondText("hello") }
            get("/limited") { call.respondText("limited") }
                .guardRateLimit(guard, requests = 5, window = 60)
        }
    }.start(wait = true)
}

See API for the full plugin behavior and decorator surface.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 17 or newer
  • Ktor 3.x (built and tested against 3.6.0)
  • Redis 6+ for the distributed features (rate limiting, IP bans, behavioral state) - configured on the engine SecurityConfig (redis_url, default redis://localhost:6379)

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
Published on Maven Central:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.guard-core:ktor-guard:1.1.0")
}

The group ID is com.guard-core (the Central Portal namespace); Kotlin packages stay com.guardcore.*.

docs.title: Engine dependency (includeBuild + dependency substitution)
docs.text:
Consumers resolve the engine artifact com.guard-core:guard-core from Maven Central. This repository's own build pins the engine from source instead: CI and local builds check out Guard-Core/guard-core-jvm at the pinned ref 7711606 as the sibling directory ./guard-core-jvm, and settings.gradle.kts substitutes the declared coordinates with the included build's projects. The declared dependency coordinates stay com.guard-core:guard-core:4.3.3 (lockstep version per the family versioning law).

git clone https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core-jvm.git guard-core-jvm
git -C guard-core-jvm checkout 7711606
./gradlew build

The engine directory resolves in order: -PguardCoreJvmDir=<path>, GUARD_CORE_JVM_DIR, ./guard-core-jvm, ../guard-core-jvm.

Set GUARD_CORE_USE_COMPOSITE=false to build without the composite: the declared coordinates then resolve from the repositories (mavenLocal first, then Maven Central) - this is how the release workflow proves the published artifact graph.

docs.title: Dependency locking
docs.text: gradle.lockfile is committed and enforced on every resolution: a dependency change without ./gradlew --write-locks fails the build. CI additionally scans the lockfile with osv-scanner (fail on any known vulnerability).

docs.title: Release runbook (ktor-guard)
docs.text: Adapter release choreography. The shared mechanics (Portal namespace, user token, GPG, publishing limits, rollback semantics) are documented once in the engine repo: guard-core-jvm docs/release.md. This file covers what differs here.

docs.title: Versioning law
docs.text:
• Artifact com.guard-core:ktor-guard; version 1.0.0 (fresh family version). The version lives in build.gradle.kts; the tag must equal it.
  • The engine lockstep pin lives in gradle/libs.versions.toml (guardCore = "4.3.3") and in the workflow env (GUARD_CORE_JVM_REF); they move only when the engine train moves.
  • Tags are bare vX.Y.z only (v1.0.0). The tag-consistency job audits this (the guard-core-rs invisible-rule incident on refs/tags/v4.3.2 is the standing lesson).
  • groupId com.guard-core; Kotlin packages stay com.guardcore.*.

docs.title: Version-flip checklist (the release PR)
docs.text:
The workflow enforces this: tagging without the flip fails tag-consistency with an explicit message.

  • [ ] build.gradle.kts: version = "1.0.0-SNAPSHOT" -> version = "1.0.0".
  • [ ] gradle/libs.versions.toml: guardCore still reads the lockstep engine version (4.3.3).
  • [ ] The GUARD_CORE_JVM_REF pin (ci.yml env + settings comments) already points at the released engine SHA (bumped at train time, per the family spec).
  • [ ] CHANGELOG.md: the unreleased section renamed to ## [1.0.0] - YYYY-MM-DD with the engine pin stated.
  • [ ] CI green on the release PR; merge it; tag the merge commit.

docs.title: Release choreography
docs.text:
Hard order: the engine artifacts MUST be live on Maven Central first. The pre-flight job checks both com.guard-core:guard-core-engine and com.guard-core:guard-core at the pinned lockstep version on repo1.maven.org and refuses to run anything if they are not (engine-before-adapters, enforced mechanically, not on the honor system).

  1. Complete the engine train first: guard-core-jvm tagged, released, Portal deployments released, repo1 answering 200 for both engine artifacts (engine docs/release.md, steps 1 and 5).
  2. Merge the version-flip PR.
  3. Tag: git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0. Gates run in order: pre-flight (engine live) -> tests at tag (composite ON, same as ci.yml) -> tag-consistency (bare tag equals the in-file version).
  4. Create the GitHub release for v1.0.0. The publish job:
  5. verifies the four secrets are set (Portal user token + GPG key);
  6. checks repo1 for this exact artifact and skips if already live (changed-only rerun safety);
  7. builds the staging bundle with GUARD_CORE_USE_COMPOSITE=false, so the engine dependency resolves from the repositories (mavenLocal, then Maven Central) - the published artifact graph, not the composite checkout;
  8. uploads the bundle to the Central Portal Publisher API (publishingType=USER_MANAGED) and polls until VALIDATED.
  9. Release the deployment in the Portal UI (central.sonatype.com, Publishing -> Deployments).
  10. Verify liveness: curl -f https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/guard-core/ktor-guard/1.0.0/ktor-guard-1.0.0.pom

docs.title: Post-release audits (per train)
docs.text:
1. Release page for v1.0.0 exists with the expected notes (per-tag audit; the php v4.3.1 lesson).
  2. repo1 answers 200 for the artifact (the same check the workflow uses).
  3. No deployment left VALIDATED/PENDING in the Portal.
  4. The GUARD_CORE_JVM_REF pin (ci.yml env + settings comments) moves to the released engine SHA AT TRAIN TIME, before the consumer tags: the adapter's at-tag tests must run against the engine that actually ships (the family spec pins this; a pin bump is an ordinary development PR).

docs.title: Rerun safety, failure recovery, rollback
docs.text: Same rules as the engine runbook: workflow_dispatch re-drives skip anything already live on repo1; a VALIDATED deployment you do not want gets Dropped in the Portal; published artifacts are immutable - no rollback after the Portal Release click, only a fix version.
